thread.title: Apple cofounder Steve Wozniak was so excited about the iconic '1984' commercial, he offered to pay $400,000 out of pocket to run it during the Super Bowl (AAPL)

author: Paige Leskin
title: Apple cofounder Steve Wozniak was so excited about the iconic '1984' commercial, he offered to pay $400,000 out of pocket to run it during the Super Bowl (AAPL)
text: Apple cofounder Steve Wozniak. David Paul Morris/Getty Images Apple cofounder Steve Wozniak recently spoke with Business Insider's Household Name podcast about the company's famous "1984" commercial. Wozniak said he liked the commercial so much when he first saw it that he offered to personally pay half of what it would cost for the ad to air during the Super Bowl — $400,000. Wozniak didn't end up having to pay for the ad, which he says is "better than any science fiction trailer." The ad, which introduced the world to Apple's Macintosh personal computer, went on to be widely celebrated and a massive success. Apple cofounder Steve Wozniak was so excited about the company's iconic "1984" commercial that he offered to pay for half of the $800,000 to secure a coveted ad spot during the Super Bowl. He was "stunned" when he heard that Apple executives had voted against airing the commercial, the Apple cofounder recently told Business Insider. "I had felt that I had just witnessed a piece of art," Wozniak says. "This was, like, better than any science fiction trailer. It was as good as it gets." On a recent episode of Business Insider's "Household Name" podcast , Wozniak and others — including former Apple CEO John Sculley — discussed how the famous 1984 Apple commercial came to fruition. The 60-second ad, which alludes to George Orwell's dystopian novel "1984," features a woman throwing a sledgehammer at a Big Brother-type figure on screen in order to save humanity from conformity. At the end of the commercial, Apple's first Macintosh computer is teased with the tagline: "You'll see why 1984 won't be like "1984." The ad aired nationally during the 1984 Super Bowl, which saw Los Angeles trounce Washington. The 60-second spot to air the ad during the Super Bowl cost $800,000 in 1984 — the equivalent of about $2 million today. To put it in perspective, a 30-second ad at this year's Super Bowl cost $5.25 million, according to CNBC . Wozniak says that when fellow cofounder Steve Jobs first showed him the ad, he was "dumbfounded." The ad conveyed the message that Wozniak wanted: Apple was leading the computing industry down a new path, and the Macintosh was the symbol of the new era. "We all believed that the Macintosh was the future of the company, and that this ad represented the way we really felt inside," Wozniak says. "That it stood up for individual creativity." It was a hit with critics and viewers, too. The commercial has been lauded as a "masterpiece" that mesmerized viewers; a "watershed event" with monumental impact. A VCR obsession Wozniak loved the ad, but the moment with Jobs had another effect on his life. Jobs played the ad on a state-of-the-art VCR, and Wozniak was smitten. It was a professional U-Matic machine, and he later used similar machines to teach himself how to edit video. "I wound up seeking out video people buying some of these U-Matic VCRs that are used in making advertisements and in the TV world, Wozniak says. "They're much smaller than the big old ancient one inch television editing systems and I ... would sit there with knobs and dial videos up on a couple of screens and press a button and the VCRs would roll and it would do an edit." This was the era before computers revolutionized movie editing, and well before Apple's own iMovie came to market. "It became a big hobby in my life, and it was all really started by Steve [Jobs] showing me this videotape, because it went into that kind of VCR." Bonus audio from our interview with Steve Wozniak: To hear the whole story, find "Household Name" on Apple Podcasts, Stitcher , or Spotify . The ad survives But while Wozniak, Jobs, and Sculley liked the ad, Apple's board of directors didn't share their love for the commercial. They voted against airing it during the Super Bowl — not because it was an issue of money, but because of concern that the ad "might offend businesspeople," Wozniak said. In the end, Wozniak didn't have to cough up $400,000 for the ad. The ad agency behind the commercial, Chiat/Day, said it was only able to sell back two of three 60-second commercial slots Apple had paid for. In the end, Apple decided to run "1984." And the rest is history. "It was just the finest ad I'd ever seen," Wozniak says.
